Transcript: In 1825 the English doctor Gideon Mantell described a new kind of giant reptile from a handful of teeth found in the south of England. The teeth looked like a much bigger version of an iguana's, so he called it Iguanodon, iguana tooth. Later, more bones turned up, including a cone-shaped spike, and Mantell did what seemed reasonable. Iguanas and some other reptiles have horns on the snout, so he put the spike on the nose. For decades, that's how Iguanodon was pictured: a huge, heavy, four-legged lizard with a horn. You can still see that version in the concrete sculptures built for the Crystal Palace park in London in the 1850s.

Then, in 1878, coal miners at Bernissart, in Belgium, hit a deposit holding dozens of Iguanodon skeletons, many of them nearly complete. And there was the spike, not on the nose at all, but on the hand. It was a thumb. The Belgian paleontologist Louis Dollo spent years on these skeletons, and he mounted them upright, standing on their hind legs and propped on their tails, like enormous kangaroos.

So the spike was fixed, and the upright animal went into textbooks for much of the twentieth century. But here's the twist. The upright pose was itself a mistake. When paleontologists looked again, around 1980, they argued that the tail was stiffened by bony tendons and couldn't have bent the way a kangaroo pose requires. The wrist bones looked built to bear weight, too. The current view is that big adults probably walked on all fours most of the time, perhaps rising onto their hind legs to run.

Which means Mantell, with his heavy four-legged animal, got the posture closer than the man who corrected him. He was wrong about the horn and roughly right about the walk.

Transcript: Say the syllables 'ba' and 'pa'. Your lips close, then open, and somewhere in there your vocal cords start vibrating. The gap between the lips opening and the voicing starting is called voice onset time. In English 'ba', voicing starts almost immediately. In 'pa' there's a delay of several hundredths of a second. The phoneticians Leigh Lisker and Arthur Abramson measured this across a range of languages in the 1960s, and it turns out to be one of the main things separating these sounds.

Now, with a speech synthesizer, you can make a whole series of syllables in which that delay grows step by step. If perception simply tracked the sound, you'd expect listeners to hear a gradual blend, something halfway in the middle. That's not what happens. In experiments of this kind, starting at Haskins Laboratories in the late 1950s, listeners heard one sound, then, past a fairly sharp boundary, the other. And they were poor at telling apart two steps on the same side of it, even when the acoustic difference was as large as one that crossed it. This was called categorical perception.

To the Haskins group it looked like evidence that speech is special, that humans have perceptual machinery built for it. Then in 1975, Patricia Kuhl and James Miller trained chinchillas, small rodents with hearing much like ours, to respond differently to 'da' and 'ta'. Tested on the steps in between, the chinchillas switched at roughly the same place English speakers do.

Chinchillas, as far as anyone knows, don't have speech. So the boundary may rest on a feature of mammal hearing in general, and languages may have tended to put their categories where hearing already draws a line. That doesn't make speech ordinary. But a sharp boundary, by itself, couldn't show that it was special.

Transcript: In 1600, a music theorist in Bologna named Giovanni Maria Artusi published a dialogue with a pointed title: on the imperfections of modern music. In it, he quoted passages from some madrigals that were circulating in manuscript, without naming the composer, and picked them apart. The composer was Claudio Monteverdi, and the most famous example came from a madrigal called 'Cruda Amarilli', cruel Amaryllis.

What bothered Artusi? Dissonance, notes that grate against each other. Renaissance rules allowed it, but under control. A dissonance had to be prepared, meaning the clashing note was already sounding before, and it had to resolve smoothly afterward. Monteverdi was letting a voice jump straight onto a clashing note, unprepared, and leave it by a leap. To Artusi, that was simply bad grammar, the work of someone who didn't know the rules or didn't care.

Here's the part people often skip: Artusi had good ears. He wasn't imagining it. Those passages really do break the rules he describes. So the argument wasn't about whether the rules were broken. It was about whether breaking them could be justified.

Monteverdi's answer came in 1605, in a short note in his fifth book of madrigals, and his brother Giulio Cesare expanded it two years later. Their claim was that there are two practices. In the first, the older one, the music rules the words. In the second, the words rule the music, so a harsh word, a cry of pain, can call for a harsh sound. And notice what they didn't say. They didn't say the old rules were wrong. Monteverdi kept writing in the old style, too, especially in church music. He asked for a second set of standards beside the first, not in place of it.

That idea, that a text can license what the rules forbid, went on to shape early opera.

Transcript: In 1600, a music theorist in Bologna named Giovanni Maria Artusi published a dialogue with a pointed title: on the imperfections of modern music. In it, he quoted passages from some madrigals that were circulating in manuscript, without naming the composer, and picked them apart. The composer was Claudio Monteverdi, and the most famous example came from a madrigal called 'Cruda Amarilli', cruel Amaryllis.

What bothered Artusi? Dissonance, notes that grate against each other. Renaissance rules allowed it, but under control. A dissonance had to be prepared, meaning the clashing note was already sounding before, and it had to resolve smoothly afterward. Monteverdi was letting a voice jump straight onto a clashing note, unprepared, and leave it by a leap. To Artusi, that was simply bad grammar, the work of someone who didn't know the rules or didn't care.

Here's the part people often skip: Artusi had good ears. He wasn't imagining it. Those passages really do break the rules he describes. So the argument wasn't about whether the rules were broken. It was about whether breaking them could be justified.

Monteverdi's answer came in 1605, in a short note in his fifth book of madrigals, and his brother Giulio Cesare expanded it two years later. Their claim was that there are two practices. In the first, the older one, the music rules the words. In the second, the words rule the music, so a harsh word, a cry of pain, can call for a harsh sound. And notice what they didn't say. They didn't say the old rules were wrong. Monteverdi kept writing in the old style, too, especially in church music. He asked for a second set of standards beside the first, not in place of it.

That idea, that a text can license what the rules forbid, went on to shape early opera.

Transcript: The word sustainability gets used for almost everything now, but in forestry it has a surprisingly specific birthplace. In 1713, Hans Carl von Carlowitz, who ran the mining administration in Saxony, in eastern Germany, published a book on forest management. Saxony's silver mines and smelters burned enormous amounts of wood and charcoal, and the forests around them were being cut faster than they grew back. Carlowitz argued that you should only cut as much as could regrow, so that the supply would last indefinitely. He used a German phrase that's usually translated as sustained use, and it's often cited as the first use of the idea in that sense.

Over the next century, German foresters turned that principle into a science. They measured how much timber a stand added each year, calculated when to cut, and planned harvests decades in advance. It was enormously influential. Forestry schools in other countries, including the United States, drew on the German model.

But think about what was actually being sustained. Not the forest, really. The yield. And the easiest way to get a predictable, measurable yield was to replant cleared land with fast-growing conifers, above all Norway spruce, often in even-aged rows, and often well outside the places where spruce grows naturally. By the numbers, these plantations were a success for a long time.

The trouble is that a forest of one species, all the same age, is fragile. Shallow-rooted spruce on the wrong soils is easily thrown down by windstorms, and in recent decades, with hotter, drier summers, bark beetles have killed huge areas of spruce in central Europe. Which is why foresters there are now trying to mix other species back in. Carlowitz's rule was sound. It just measured one thing, the wood, and two centuries of foresters took very good care of that one thing.

Transcript: For most of history, the autumn disappearance of birds was a real puzzle. Aristotle suggested that some birds change into other species with the seasons, and that others hide away and become dormant. In 1555 the Swedish churchman Olaus Magnus wrote that fishermen in the north sometimes pulled up swallows clustered together in the mud at the bottom of lakes, where, he said, they spent the winter. That idea had defenders well into the eighteenth century. Even the naturalist Carl Linnaeus seems to have accepted it.

What helped settle it was, of all things, an arrow. In 1822, a white stork was shot in northern Germany with a long wooden arrow stuck clean through its neck. The arrow was of a central African type. The bird had been wounded in Africa, survived, and flown thousands of kilometers back to Europe with the shaft still in it. It's preserved in Rostock, and German has a word for it, Pfeilstorch, arrow stork. Two dozen or so more have been recorded since. Hard to argue that storks winter in mud after that.

So migration won, and hibernating birds went into the same box as birds changing species. Except, in 1946, a naturalist named Edmund Jaeger found a common poorwill, a small nightjar-like bird, wedged in a rock crevice in the California desert in the middle of winter. It was cold and barely breathing. He came back the following winters and found it there again. That bird was in a deep torpor that could last for weeks. It's still the only bird known to do anything this close to true hibernation. The Hopi, by one account, already had a name for it meaning the sleeping one.

So the swallows in the mud were a myth. But the claim that no bird ever sleeps through the winter turned out to be too strong.

Transcript: If you look at European maps of North America from the sixteenth century, California is usually drawn as part of the mainland. That's correct. In 1539, a Spanish expedition under Francisco de Ulloa sailed to the head of the Gulf of California and found that it closed off. Baja California was a peninsula, and many maps showed it that way.

Then, in the early seventeenth century, something strange happens. California detaches. Starting around the 1620s, on maps printed in Amsterdam and London, it becomes a long island, cut off from the continent by a strait. One of the most widely copied versions appeared in 1625, on a map attributed to the English mathematician Henry Briggs. Where the idea came from isn't entirely clear. One source seems to have been a Spanish friar, Antonio de la Ascensión, who sailed with an expedition up the Pacific coast in 1602. There's also a story that the Dutch captured a Spanish chart showing the island, but that's hard to confirm.

What's harder to explain is how long it lasted. The island stayed on many maps for over a century. That's partly how the map trade worked. Engravers copied from each other constantly, and a dramatic island sold better than a plain coastline. Around 1700, the Jesuit missionary Eusebio Kino traveled overland near the head of the gulf and reported that you could walk to California. Even that didn't settle it right away. In 1747 the Spanish king, Ferdinand the Sixth, issued a decree declaring flatly that California is not an island.

We tend to imagine the history of maps as a steady march toward accuracy. This case runs the other way. The correct picture came first, a worse one replaced it, and the error survived largely because mapmakers trusted earlier maps more than new reports.

Transcript: If you look at European maps of North America from the sixteenth century, California is usually drawn as part of the mainland. That's correct. In 1539, a Spanish expedition under Francisco de Ulloa sailed to the head of the Gulf of California and found that it closed off. Baja California was a peninsula, and many maps showed it that way.

Then, in the early seventeenth century, something strange happens. California detaches. Starting around the 1620s, on maps printed in Amsterdam and London, it becomes a long island, cut off from the continent by a strait. One of the most widely copied versions appeared in 1625, on a map attributed to the English mathematician Henry Briggs. Where the idea came from isn't entirely clear. One source seems to have been a Spanish friar, Antonio de la Ascensión, who sailed with an expedition up the Pacific coast in 1602. There's also a story that the Dutch captured a Spanish chart showing the island, but that's hard to confirm.

What's harder to explain is how long it lasted. The island stayed on many maps for over a century. That's partly how the map trade worked. Engravers copied from each other constantly, and a dramatic island sold better than a plain coastline. Around 1700, the Jesuit missionary Eusebio Kino traveled overland near the head of the gulf and reported that you could walk to California. Even that didn't settle it right away. In 1747 the Spanish king, Ferdinand the Sixth, issued a decree declaring flatly that California is not an island.

We tend to imagine the history of maps as a steady march toward accuracy. This case runs the other way. The correct picture came first, a worse one replaced it, and the error survived largely because mapmakers trusted earlier maps more than new reports.

Transcript: For a long time, oceanographers treated sailors' stories about giant waves the way you might treat fishing stories. A captain would come back describing a wall of water, maybe thirty meters high, rising out of a fairly ordinary sea, and the response was, well, you were frightened, and it was dark. The skepticism had a real basis. The standard model treated the sea surface as many independent waves added together. Now and then crests line up and you get a big one, but the math put a firm limit on how often. A wave more than twice the height of the large waves around it should turn up only very rarely, perhaps once in thousands of years at any given spot.

Then, on New Year's Day 1995, a laser on the Draupner gas platform in the North Sea measured one. The surrounding waves were around twelve meters, and a single wave reached about twenty-six. It wasn't a story anymore. It was a number on an instrument. A few years later, a European project used satellite radar to scan the oceans and reportedly found more than ten waves above twenty-five meters in about three weeks.

So the model was wrong somewhere. One proposal was that, in some conditions, a wave can draw energy from its neighbors and grow far beyond what simple adding allows. That works nicely in long, narrow lab tanks. But in 2018, researchers recreated the Draupner wave in a large circular tank, and what mattered seemed to be two wave systems crossing at a wide angle. Crossing seas, it appears, let a wave grow steeper before it breaks.

What I'd stress is that the sailors were never the ones who needed correcting. Their reports were data all along. The mistake was trusting a model's assumption over the people who'd actually been out there.

Transcript: Economists used to have a simple view of exercise. If you buy a gym membership, it's because the benefits are worth the price to you, and you'll go about as often as you planned. Then in 2006, Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier looked at records from thousands of members of American health clubs. People who chose a monthly contract, about seventy dollars, went a little over four times a month on average. That works out to roughly seventeen dollars a visit, when the same clubs sold ten-visit passes at about ten dollars a visit. Many members were, in effect, paying not to go. The usual reading is that people are overconfident about their future selves. When they sign up, they picture someone who'll go three times a week.

If that's the problem, there's an obvious remedy. Repetition builds habits, so pay people to go until the routine sticks. In a 2009 study, Gary Charness and Uri Gneezy paid university students to attend a gym eight times in one month. Afterward, the students who hadn't been regular gym-goers kept going noticeably more than a comparison group, even with the money gone. It looked as if a habit had been bought.

The trouble came with scale. Later and much larger studies, including one with over sixty thousand members of a gym chain testing more than fifty different programs, found that many programs raised attendance while they ran, but much of the gain seemed to fade within weeks of the end.

Why? My own reading, and it's only a reading, is that a paid visit is a decision, not a habit. Habits, as psychologists describe them, are responses set off by a stable cue, the same time, the same place, so that you stop deciding at all. Paying people rewards the decision. It may not build the cue.

Transcript: Medieval master masons built enormous stone churches with no structural theory in our sense. No calculus, no formulas for stress. What they had were rules of proportion, passed from master to apprentice and closely guarded. In one German mason's manual from around 1500, for example, the size of a buttress follows from the width of the vault it supports. Rules like that are purely geometric. They say nothing about how strong the stone is, or how heavy.

For a long time, engineers read this as a sign that the masons worked by trial and error, and that the cathedrals we admire are simply the ones that happened not to fall. And there were failures. The choir at Beauvais, built with one of the highest vaults ever attempted, partly collapsed in 1284 and had to be rebuilt with extra supports.

But in the 1960s the engineer Jacques Heyman made an argument that turned this around. Stone is enormously strong when it's squeezed. In a typical cathedral, the stresses are only a small fraction of what the stone can bear. So masonry almost never fails by crushing. It fails when the shape is wrong, when the path the forces follow wanders outside the masonry and the structure folds up like a hinged chain. And whether that happens depends on geometry. A stable arch built at twice the size is, to a good approximation, still stable.

So a proportional rule isn't a crude stand-in for real theory. For masonry, it's close to the right theory. A rule that held up on one church should hold up on a larger one with the same proportions. Where it could fail was when builders pushed past proportions anyone had tried, which is one way to read Beauvais. The masons weren't lucky. They were measuring the thing that mattered.

Transcript: If you owned a cordless phone or an early laptop in the 1990s, someone probably told you to run the battery all the way down before recharging it. Otherwise, the story went, the battery would remember the shorter cycle and lose capacity. This advice grew from a real observation. Nickel-cadmium cells in satellites were discharged to almost exactly the same depth on every orbit, and engineers noticed that, after many such cycles, the voltage dropped sharply at that point, as if the cell had learned where to stop.

But that pattern needs precise, identical cycles, which almost nobody's phone ever had. Most of what consumers blamed on memory seems to have been something else, usually called voltage depression. Leave a nickel-cadmium battery on a charger for days, and crystals in the cadmium electrode can grow larger, which lowers the voltage. Devices read that lower voltage as empty. A few full discharges could often reverse it, which is probably why the folk advice seemed to work.

Then lithium-ion batteries took over, and the advice became actively harmful. Draining a lithium-ion cell completely stresses it, and so does sitting at full charge, especially in heat. Shallow, partial cycles are gentler. So the standard line became that lithium batteries have no memory at all.

That turned out to be a little too strong. In 2013, a team at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Switzerland, working with Toyota, reported a small memory effect in one lithium-ion chemistry, lithium iron phosphate, which is used in some electric vehicles. After a partial charge, the voltage showed a tiny bump at the point where the earlier cycle had stopped. It doesn't seem to cost capacity, but it could mislead the software that estimates how much charge is left. Two corrections, then, pointing in opposite directions.

Transcript: On a summer evening in much of North America, most of the flashes you see come from males, flying low and signaling. Each species of the genus Photinus has its own pattern, one long flash, say, or a pair of quick ones. A female perched in the grass watches, and if the pattern is right, she answers. But the feature that matters most may not be her flash itself. It's the timing. In a number of species, the female answers after a fairly fixed delay, a second or two depending on the species and the temperature, and the male uses that delay to judge whether she's one of his own kind.

You'd think a code based on timing would be private. It isn't. In the 1960s the biologist James Lloyd documented females of a different genus, Photuris, sitting in the grass and answering Photinus males with the right delay. When a male lands to court, she grabs him and eats him. Lloyd called them femmes fatales. Some of these females can apparently switch their replies to match whichever prey species is flying nearby.

The obvious explanation is food. Here's the part that surprised researchers. Photinus fireflies contain defensive chemicals, steroids called lucibufagins, that make them distasteful to spiders and birds. Photuris fireflies don't seem able to make these chemicals themselves. In work published in the late 1990s, Thomas Eisner and colleagues showed that Photuris females that had eaten Photinus took up the chemicals and were rejected more often by spiders. So the female isn't only getting a meal. She's acquiring her prey's protection.

Which says something about signals in general. A signal anyone can produce cheaply can be faked, and a flash costs almost nothing to fake. The male's attention to timing helps him find a mate. It can't save him from a predator that has learned the timing.

Transcript: For most of history, an hour wasn't a fixed length of time. In ancient Rome, and in much of medieval Europe, the period of daylight was divided into twelve hours, whatever its length. So a summer hour in Rome lasted roughly an hour and a quarter of ours, and a winter hour about three quarters. These are called temporal hours. A sundial shows them more or less automatically, while water clocks had to be adjusted through the year.

The usual story is that the mechanical clock killed them off. The first weight-driven clocks appeared in Europe around the end of the thirteenth century, using a device called an escapement that releases the gears in steady, equal beats. A machine like that naturally counts equal hours, and over the fourteenth century, towns that installed public clocks began running their days by equal hours, struck on a bell. Machine first, new hour after.

But there are two problems with putting it that way. First, equal hours weren't new. Greek astronomers had used them in their calculations more than a thousand years earlier. The idea was available. Daily life just hadn't wanted it.

Second, and more telling, look at Japan. European clocks reached Japan with missionaries in the sixteenth century, and Japanese clockmakers took up the mechanism. But Japan kept unequal hours, six divisions of daylight and six of night. So they changed the machine. Some clocks had two balance bars, one regulating the day and one the night, switching over automatically at dawn and dusk, and the weights were moved every couple of weeks as the seasons shifted.
